bib.title: The Jackknife and the Bootstrap (Chapter 10, Computer Age Statistical Inference)

question: How can standard errors of arbitrary statistics be estimated by computation (jackknife, bootstrap) instead of Taylor-series formulas?
contributions: Defines jackknife SE (10.6) and nonparametric bootstrap SE (10.16) as plug-in estimates
Unifies them as resampling plans on the simplex
Parametric bootstrap, multisample bootstrap, moving blocks, Bayesian bootstrap
Influence functions and robust (trimmed mean) estimation

results.claim: Eigenratio of the 22-student, 5-test score data is 0.693; nonparametric bootstrap SE is 0.075 (B=2000).
results.setup: Student score data, n=22, five tests, statistic = largest eigenvalue / sum of eigenvalues, B=2000 nonparametric bootstrap replications

results.claim: Jackknife SE for the eigenratio is larger than the bootstrap SE.
results.quote: The jackknife (10.6) gave a bigger estimate,

results.claim: Eigenvalues of the student score correlation matrix.

results.claim: Parametric bootstrap (5-dim normal MLE) gives a smaller eigenratio SE than nonparametric.
results.setup: Student score data n=22, B=2000 replications from N5(xbar, Sigma-hat MLE); nonparametric 0.075; data has at least one notable outlier so normality is doubtful
results.quote: with bseboot D 0:070 compared with the nonparametric estimate

results.claim: Jackknife-after-bootstrap puts the SE of the bootstrap SE 0.075 at 0.022, so 0.075 is not very accurate with n=22.
results.setup: Eigenratio, the original B=2000 replications reused; about 37% of bootstrap samples omit any given xi

results.claim: Jackknife SE for the correlation of age and tot in the kidney data equals the nonparametric bootstrap SE (0.058); Taylor-series formula gives 0.057.
results.setup: Kidney data, n=157 pairs (age, tot), sample correlation -0.572
results.note: Taylor value 0.057 printed on p.157 as 'bse D 0:057'
results.quote: gave bsejack D 0:058 for the accuracy

results.claim: Jackknife overstates variability of the lowess curve at age 25, while bootstrap SEs (B=500) remain dependable.
results.setup: Kidney data lowess curve evaluated at ages 20,25,...,85; Fig 10.1; B=500

results.claim: For the sample mean, the jackknife SE equals the classic formula; the ideal bootstrap variance differs by the factor (n-1)/n.
results.quote: exactly the same as the classic formula (1.2).

results.claim: Standard error of a sample mean of the 47 ALL scores: mean 0.752, se 0.040.
B=200 replications is usually sufficient for a bootstrap SE; 1000 to 2000 are needed for bootstrap confidence intervals.
results.setup: Standard errors; Efron and Tibshirani 1993 sec 6.4 cited. Smaller numbers, 25 or even less, can be useful when resampling is expensive

results.claim: The eigenratio example used 10 times more bootstraps than needed for the SE.
results.setup: Needed only for Chapter 11 confidence intervals

results.claim: Number of distinct bootstrap samples is C(2n-1, n): 92,378 for n=10, 6.9e10 for n=20; only 10 for n=3.
results.quote: For n D 10 this is already 92,378

results.claim: Jackknife points lie at distance 1/sqrt(n(n-1)) from P0, whereas bootstrap vectors are about sqrt(n) times further (sqrt((n-1)/n^2)).
results.quote: an order of magnitude pn times further than (10.33).

results.claim: Multisample bootstrap SE of the AML minus ALL median difference is 0.074; 0.235 is 3.18 SE above zero, close to the two-sample t of 3.01.
results.setup: AML n=25 and ALL n=47 resampled separately, B=500; median diff 0.968-0.733=0.235

results.claim: Two-sample t-statistic on mean differences is 3.01.
Bootstrap SEs for the gfr density grow with polynomial degrees of freedom; df 3 or 4 suggested as compromise. Parametric (Poisson, Lindsey method) B=200.
results.setup: gfr histogram, n=211, K=32 bins width 3 from 13 to 109, Poisson regression df=2..7; df=3 column

results.claim: Nonparametric (binomial bin count) SE at gfr 47.5 is far larger than parametric SEs, showing the cost of the highly parameterized nonparametric approach.
results.table: Table 10.2, row gfr 47.5, column Nonparametric standard error

results.claim: Trimmed mean with trim 0.2 has the smallest bootstrap SD (0.035) for the 47 ALL scores, versus 0.040 for the mean.
results.setup: 47 ALL scores, B=1000 per trim value; mean 0.720
results.table: Table 10.3, row trim .2, column Bootstrap sd

results.claim: Median (trim 0.5) has bootstrap sd 0.053, and the influence-function/IJ SE estimate fails for the median.
results.table: Table 10.3, row Median .5, column Bootstrap sd

results.claim: Jackknife SE is upwardly biased for the true SE (Efron and Stein 1981) and is unreliable for non-smooth statistics such as the median.
results.quote: The jackknife standard error is upwardly biased as an estimate of the true standard error.

results.claim: Bayesian bootstrap weights P=G/sum G (G iid Exp(1)) have covariance factor 1/(n+1), almost identical to bootstrap 1/n.
results.quote: This is almost identical to the mean and covariance of bootstrap resamples

limits: Jackknife depends on local derivatives and fails for unsmooth statistics (lowess at age 25, median).
Bootstrap SE based on n=22 is itself noisy (jackknife-after-bootstrap SE 0.022).
Parametric bootstrap SE (0.070) is doubtful because the data has a notable outlier.
Selecting an estimator from Table 10.3 affects accuracy, deferred to Chapter 20.
Bootstrap confidence intervals are deferred to Chapter 11; B needs 1000-2000 there.
Moving blocks bootstrap block length m is not specified beyond 'large enough'.
practices: Use B=200 replications for a bootstrap SE; 1000-2000 for bootstrap confidence intervals (p.161).
For two groups, resample within each group to keep group sizes fixed (p.167).
For time series use the moving blocks bootstrap with block length m large enough that correlations beyond m are negligible (p.168).
Inspect the bootstrap histogram before trusting +-1.96 se normal intervals (p.162).
Use the parametric bootstrap when a model is credible; it regularizes but depends on the model (p.172).
Use the bootstrap rather than influence-function SEs for the median (p.177).

figures.caption: The lowess curve for the kidney data of Figure 1.2. Vertical bars indicate ±2 standard errors: jackknife (10.6) blue dashed; bootstrap (10.16) red solid. The jackknife greatly overestimates variability at age 25.
figures.why: Shows the jackknife failing on an unsmooth statistic

figures.caption: Histogram of B = 2000 bootstrap replications θ* for the eigenratio statistic (10.22) for the student score data. The vertical black line is at θ̂ = .693. The long left tail shows that normality is a dangerous assumption in this case.
figures.why: Bootstrap histogram reveals non-normality; SEs bootstrap .075, jackknife .083

figures.caption: Resampling simplex for sample size n = 3. The center point is P0 (10.26); the green circles are the jackknife points P(i) (10.28); triples indicate bootstrap resampling numbers (N1, N2, N3) (10.29). The bootstrap probabilities are 6/27 for P0, 1/27 for each corner point, and 3/27 for each of the six starred points.
figures.why: Geometric unification of jackknife and bootstrap

figures.caption: B = 500 bootstrap replications for the median difference between the AML and ALL scores in Figure 1.4, giving se_boot = 0.074. The observed value mediff = 0.235 (vertical black line) is more than 3 standard errors above zero.

The gfr data of Figure 5.7 (histogram). Curves show the MLE fits from polynomial Poisson models, for degrees of freedom df = 2, 3, ..., 7. The points on the curves show the fits computed at the centers x(j) of the bins, with the responses being the counts in the bins. The dashes at the base of the plot show the nine gfr values appearing in Table 10.2.
figures.why: Parametric model fits used for the parametric bootstrap

figures.caption: Eigenratio example, student score data. Solid histogram B = 2000 parametric bootstrap replications θ* from the five-dimensional normal MLE; line histogram the 2000 nonparametric replications of Figure 10.2. MLE θ̂ = .693 is vertical red line.
figures.why: Parametric vs nonparametric bootstrap SE (.070 vs .075)

figures.caption: Empirical influence functions for the 47 leukemia ALL scores of Figure 1.4. The two dashed curves are IF_α(x) for the trimmed means (10.68), for α = 0.2 and α = 0.4. The solid curve is IF(x) for the sample mean x̄ (10.60).

Correlation matrix for the student score data. The eigenvalues are 3.463, 0.660, 0.447, 0.234, and 0.197. The eigenratio statistic θ̂ = 0.693, and its bootstrap standard error estimate is 0.075 (B = 2000).
